survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2015 science domain data for Korea and restricts the analytic sample to high school students only, excluding students with systematic missing values in science-related questionnaire items (final N=4,634). The manuscript does not report whether PISA sampling/student weights or replicate weights were applied in the random-forest training and evaluation, nor does it name any weight variables. Because the analysis is an ensemble random forest with hybrid sampling (ROSE) and hyper-ensemble aggregation, the authors’ weighting approach (if any) is not transparent; readers should treat the results as predictive patterns rather than population-representative estimates unless weights are confirmed. For replication, analysts should use the appropriate PISA student/sampling weights (and replicate weights if variance estimation is required) from the PISA international database, and ensure the weighting/variance procedure is compatible with the resampling strategy used for class imbalance.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: PISA 2015 assesses 15-year-old students; the study selects only high school students in Korea (excluding middle school students) to match curriculum/system differences. From the selected students, 424 students with systematic missing values in science-related questionnaire items were excluded. The final analytic sample therefore contains 4,634 high school students with an effective response rate of ≥97% on the questionnaire items used as predictors.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Science (Korea, high school students; achievement groups from science cognitive domain proficiency levels 1–6)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest (hyper-ensemble across 100 balanced datasets; 50,000 trees per model; 70% train / remaining test): Accuracy mean=0.84 (range 0.79–0.89), Sensitivity mean=0.86 (0.76–0.92), Specificity mean=0.81 (0.71–0.91), AUC mean=0.84 (0.80–0.87). Additional analysis (Low-achievement group vs moderate group (science)): Random Forest (hyper-ensemble across 100 balanced datasets; 50,000 trees per model; 70% train / remaining test): Accuracy mean=0.84 (range 0.77–0.89), Sensitivity mean=0.86 (0.74–0.94), Specificity mean=0.82 (0.73–0.91), AUC mean=0.84 (0.81–0.88).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Science data for Korea (high school students) the study leveraged read books on scientific discoveries, science fiction exposure, science club participation, teacher-directed demonstrations of ideas, and inquiry-based designing experiments to predict membership in the high-achievement group versus the moderate group, finding that these science activity and instructional-strategy variables had the highest mean importance and produced strong classification performance (AUC≈0.84). This indicates that strengthening early and ongoing science engagement (e.g., reading and clubs) together with inquiry and adaptive instructional practices may increase the likelihood of students reaching high science proficiency, though the study is predictive and cannot establish causality.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2015 science domain data for Korea, restricting the sample to high school students and excluding 424 students with systematic missing values in science-related questionnaire items, yielding 4,634 students. Science achievement groups were created from PISA science cognitive domain proficiency levels (1–6), collapsing them into high (levels 5–6), moderate (2–4), and low (1). Using an educational data mining approach, the authors trained random-forest classifiers with a hyper-ensemble strategy: 100 balanced datasets were generated via ROSE hybrid sampling to address class imbalance, and each model used 50,000 trees with 70% training and the remainder for testing. For both high-vs-moderate and low-vs-moderate predictions, performance was consistently high (AUC mean ≈0.84; accuracy mean ≈0.84; sensitivity mean ≈0.86). Top predictors included science reading/club participation and instructional strategies (inquiry, adaptive instruction, and perceived feedback). The authors note that, due to the nature of PISA questionnaire data, causal relationships cannot be concluded.
